title: Identifying Operational & Financial Risk (CMA P2-D · feeds AUD)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — name the risk before you can manage it

You cannot mitigate what you have not identified. MBG's exposures span two broad families: operational risk (failures of people, process, systems, or external events) and financial risk (liquidity, credit, and market). The unreconciled $95,000.00 in Account 111 is a process risk; the $400,000.00 stranded across 7 dormant accounts is a liquidity risk; volatile lumber and steel prices are a market risk. This week is about systematically surfacing and rating them.

Operational risk

Operational risk arises from inadequate or failed internal processes, people, and systems, or from external events. For MBG: reconciling across JCS, Ledgerline, and PayStream creates interface and cutoff risk; an unreconciled clearing account signals a process control gap; reliance on a few key people creates key-person risk; and weather, permitting, and supply disruptions are external operational risks. These rarely show up as a single ledger number, which is why they are easy to under-weight.

Financial risk

Financial risk has three classic forms. Liquidity risk — the inability to meet obligations as they come due — is MBG's most pressing, with usable cash thinned by the dormant balances. Credit risk — a customer, owner, or general contractor failing to pay — is amplified in construction by retainage held until completion. Market risk covers interest-rate risk on floating debt, foreign-exchange risk on cross-border purchases (month 7, week 4), and commodity/material-price risk on lumber, steel, and fuel. A fixed-price contract signed before a material spike converts market risk directly into margin risk.

Identification techniques

Disciplined identification uses several tools: a risk register (the catalog from week 1), brainstorming and scenario analysis, process walkthroughs, loss-event data, and key risk indicators (KRIs) — forward-looking metrics that warn before a risk materializes (for example, days of usable cash, count of expired certificates of insurance, or the aging of unreconciled clearing items). KRIs differ from key performance indicators: a KPI measures achievement, a KRI signals emerging exposure.

Rating risk — the heat map

Each identified risk is rated on two axes: likelihood (how probable) and impact (how severe). Plotting likelihood × impact on a heat map prioritizes attention — high-likelihood, high-impact risks (red) demand immediate response, while low-likelihood, low-impact risks (green) may be accepted. MBG's expired-COI exposure rates high on impact (an uninsured claim on an active job would be severe), while its likelihood must be assessed from actual exposure data — the number of affected active jobs and the claim history — rather than assumed from the deficiency itself. A known control gap of this potential severity still warrants the urgent reduce-and-transfer response from week 1, even before the likelihood is quantified.

A risk taxonomy and structured identification

Organizing exposures into a taxonomy keeps identification from missing whole categories. A common scheme: strategic risk (wrong markets, demand shifts, competitor moves), operational risk (process, people, systems, external events — MBG's multi-system reconciliation and key-person dependence), financial risk (liquidity, credit, market), compliance/legal risk (the expired COIs, lien and labor law), and hazard risk (fire, weather, jobsite injury). Walking the taxonomy deliberately surfaces risks that a single brainstorming session would skip, and it maps cleanly onto the insurance and hedging responses that follow.

Identification draws on several techniques used together: facilitated risk workshops and interviews, historical loss-event data, process walkthroughs, SWOT and scenario analysis, and external scanning for emerging risks the firm has never experienced. A useful structuring tool is bow-tie analysis: place the risk event in the center, list its causes on the left with the preventive controls between them, and its consequences on the right with the mitigating controls — a single picture of how a risk arises and how it is contained. For a jobsite fall, the left side is the hazards and the safety controls that prevent it; the right side is injury, delay, and claim, with insurance and emergency response as the mitigations.

Designing key risk indicators

A good KRI is leading, not lagging — it warns before the loss. Days of usable cash falling toward the bonding-required floor, the count and aging of expired certificates of insurance, the trend in unreconciled clearing items, and the concentration of backlog in one customer are all forward-looking signals for MBG. Each KRI needs a defined threshold and an owner who acts when it is breached; an indicator no one is accountable for is decoration. The art is choosing a small set of indicators that genuinely predict the exposures that matter, rather than a dashboard so crowded that the real warnings are lost.

From identification to a rated register

Identification ends by placing each risk on the likelihood-by-impact map and recording its inherent rating, the controls in place, and the residual rating after those controls. MBG's expired-COI exposure rates high on impact, with its likelihood assessed from exposure data rather than assumed from the deficiency itself; a working compliance-tracking control and valid insurance lower the residual rating into an acceptable zone. The register is then sorted by residual rating so management's attention and budget go to the red-zone risks first — the discipline that turns a long list of worries into a prioritized program.

Beyond likelihood and impact

Two dimensions beyond the basic heat map sharpen prioritization. Velocity (or speed of onset) measures how quickly a risk moves from emergence to impact: a liquidity squeeze can arrive in days, while a slow erosion of competitiveness plays out over years, and a fast, high-impact risk deserves more pre-positioned response than its likelihood-impact score alone suggests. Persistence measures how long the impact lasts once it hits. A jobsite injury and a lost key client both rate high on impact, but one is a contained event and the other reshapes the business for years; the response budget should reflect that difference.

Risks also interrelate. They rarely arrive one at a time: a construction downturn simultaneously slows collections (liquidity), strains marginal subcontractors (credit and performance), and pressures margins (strategic), and these correlations are exactly what make a bad year severe rather than merely inconvenient. Identification that treats each risk as independent understates the real exposure, which is why scenario analysis — stringing several plausible risks into one coherent story — belongs alongside the line-by-line register. The goal of identification is not a longer list; it is a prioritized, interconnected map that points management's limited attention and budget at the exposures most able to threaten MBG's objectives. Identification is therefore the foundation of everything that follows: a risk that is never named can never be rated, assigned an owner, mitigated, monitored, or reported — it simply waits, unmanaged, until the day it becomes a loss someone then has to explain. Naming the exposure clearly and completely is the single cheapest risk control there is, and the one on which every later step depends.

CPA Crossover — AUD

AUD's risk-assessment standards mirror this: identify risks of material misstatement by understanding the entity and its environment, then assess likelihood and magnitude. The operational/financial taxonomy and the likelihood-times-impact rating are directly transferable to audit risk assessment.

Practice and recap

  1. Classify each exposure as operational or financial (liquidity, credit, or market).
  2. Use a register, scenarios, loss data, and KRIs to surface risks.
  3. Rate each on likelihood and impact and place it on a heat map.
  4. Prioritize red-zone risks for immediate response.

Recap: MBG's risks split into operational (process, systems, people, external) and financial (liquidity, credit, market). Identification tools plus a likelihood-by-impact heat map turn a vague sense of exposure into a ranked, actionable list — with expired COIs rating high on impact and their likelihood pending assessment from exposure data — not automatically red on the deficiency alone.

flashcards.back: Retainage is held until completion, extending exposure to customer/owner default.

flashcards.front: Material-price volatility is which risk type?
flashcards.back: Market risk (commodity/price); a fixed-price contract turns it into margin risk.

questions.q: An unreconciled $95,000.00 clearing account is primarily an example of:
questions.explain: A control/process gap in reconciliation is an operational risk.

questions.q: The inability to meet obligations as they come due is:
questions.explain: Liquidity risk is the inability to meet obligations when due.

questions.q: Volatile lumber and steel prices on a fixed-price contract represent:
questions.explain: Material-price volatility is market risk; under a fixed price it becomes margin risk.

questions.q: A risk heat map plots each risk on which two axes?
questions.explain: Heat maps rate likelihood against impact to prioritize response.

questions.q: A key risk indicator (KRI) differs from a KPI because it:
choices: Signals emerging exposure before a risk materializes
questions.explain: A KRI is forward-looking and warns of emerging risk; a KPI measures performance achieved.

questions.q: Retainage withheld until completion most directly increases which risk?
questions.explain: Holding retainage extends the period of exposure to a customer/owner default — credit risk.

questions.q: MBG has expired certificates of insurance on some active jobs. How should the claim risk be rated on a heat map?
choices: Automatically high-likelihood because the certificates are expired
High impact, with likelihood assessed from actual exposure data (affected jobs, claim history)
questions.explain: The control deficiency is certain and the impact is high, but claim likelihood must be assessed from exposure data, not assumed high from the deficiency alone.
